R1.commandsIntro: Run the named script from Code. For R7 and R8, type the commands at the MicroPython REPL after the script starts. The grey label shows where each action happens.
R1.title: Wire PN532
R1.heading: Connect and identify the PN532 V3
R1.goal: Replace the RC522 SPI wiring with four PN532 I²C wires and verify the reader firmware before using a card.
R1.goalLine: Read a stable PN532 firmware version three times on the Pulsar C5.
goalCheck: Three lines report IC 0x32 without a bus or checksum error.

0.title: How the I²C check works
body: The Pulsar C5 scans the I²C bus on GPIO1 (SDA) and GPIO6 (SCL). A correctly wired PN532 in I²C mode answers at the 7-bit address 0x24.

The script requests the chip and firmware version three times, then prepares the reader for card detection. Repeated matching answers show that commands and responses can travel over the bus before a card is involved.

0.does: Scans I²C, reads the PN532 firmware three times and configures the reader.
0.see: 0x24 appears in the scan and all three lines show IC 0x32.

steps: Unplug USB. Set PN532 V3 switch 1 ON and switch 2 OFF. Wire the four I²C pins as in R1. Open Code, install pn532.py once, and connect the MicroPython REPL.
Run rfid_r1_pn532.py with no card nearby.
Check address 0x24 and compare the three firmware readings.
R1.note: Use the PN532's I²C SDA/SCL pins, not its SPI pins. MicroPython shows 7-bit address 0x24; NXP's manual calls its 8-bit write address 0x48. QWIIC GPIO1/6 needs pull-ups on the module or wiring. Power the module from 3V3.

R2.commandsIntro: Run the named script from Code. For R7 and R8, type the commands at the MicroPython REPL after the script starts. The grey label shows where each action happens.
R2.title: Wake a card
R2.heading: Detect one ISO14443-A card
R2.goal: Activate one nearby card and read its UID, ATQA and SAK. Lift it to observe removal.
R2.goalLine: See one detection per placement and a removal when the card leaves the antenna.
goalCheck: A card prints UID, ATQA and SAK.

0.title: How card detection works
body: The PN532 repeatedly searches for one ISO14443-A target. When a card enters the antenna field, it activates the card and returns its UID, ATQA and SAK to MicroPython.
The script remembers the last UID, so a card held in place prints once. After three scans without a card it prints Card removed; presenting it again starts a new detection.

0.does: Polls the PN532 and prints a new card's UID, ATQA and SAK once.
0.see: One UID line appears when you place the card.

1.does: Lets three scans pass without a detected card, clearing the remembered UID.
1.see: Card removed appears; the next placement prints the UID again.

steps: Unplug USB. Set PN532 V3 switch 1 ON and switch 2 OFF. Wire the four I²C pins as in R1. Open Code, install pn532.py once, and connect the MicroPython REPL.
Run rfid_r2_pn532.py and place one card flat on the antenna.
Lift it and present it again; compare the UIDs.
R2.note: A UID identifies a card for this exercise but is not a secure credential. This script asks the PN532 for one target per scan.

R3.commandsIntro: Run the named script from Code. For R7 and R8, type the commands at the MicroPython REPL after the script starts. The grey label shows where each action happens.
R3.title: Who's there
R3.heading: Build a sequential card inventory
R3.goal: Present several cards one at a time and count each unique UID.
R3.goalLine: Make an inventory of at least two different cards.
goalCheck: Each distinct card appears in the list.
Presenting one again increases its count.

0.title: How the inventory works
body: Each scan asks the PN532 to select one card. The script converts its UID to text and uses that UID as a key in a dictionary of encounter counts.
A card held on the antenna is counted only once until it is lifted. Presenting it again increases its count; pressing Ctrl+C prints the complete list. Cards are read one at a time.

0.does: Adds each newly presented UID to the inventory or increases its count.
0.see: Each tap prints the UID, SAK and number of times seen.

1.does: Stops the scan loop and prints the saved counts.
1.see: Unique cards and one count per UID appear.

steps: Unplug USB. Set PN532 V3 switch 1 ON and switch 2 OFF. Wire the four I²C pins as in R1. Open Code, install pn532.py once, and connect the MicroPython REPL.
Run rfid_r3_pn532.py. Tap two cards separately and lift each between taps.
Press Ctrl+C to print the final counts.
R3.note: This is a sequential inventory, not simultaneous reading of overlapping tags. ISO14443-A UIDs may be 4, 7 or 10 bytes.

R4.commandsIntro: Run the named script from Code. For R7 and R8, type the commands at the MicroPython REPL after the script starts. The grey label shows where each action happens.
R4.title: Inside a tag
R4.heading: Read user memory
R4.goal: Read MIFARE Classic block 4 with the factory Key A, or Type 2 pages 8–11.
R4.goalLine: See 16 data bytes from a tag you own without changing them.
goalCheck: The script prints Classic block 4 or Type 2 pages 8–11.

0.title: How a memory read works
body: After detecting a tag, the script uses its response to choose a supported memory path. For MIFARE Classic it authenticates sector 1 with Key A or B, then reads data block 4. For a supported Type 2 tag it reads pages 8–11.
Both paths return 16 data bytes. A Classic authentication error 0x14 means the chosen sector key did not open that block; the script reports the error and makes no memory change.

0.does: Detects the tag, authenticates Classic when needed and reads 16 user-data bytes.
0.see: Classic data block 4 or Type 2 pages 8-11 followed by 16 hex bytes.

steps: Unplug USB. Set PN532 V3 switch 1 ON and switch 2 OFF. Wire the four I²C pins as in R1. Open Code, install pn532.py once, and connect the MicroPython REPL.
Reinstall the updated pn532.py on the board, then run rfid_r4_pn532.py and present one test tag.
Note its SAK and the 16 printed data bytes. If PN532 reports 0x14, enter a known sector 1 key in CLASSIC_KEY and select Key A or B with CLASSIC_KEY_TYPE.
R4.note: PN532 status 0x14 means MIFARE Classic authentication failed. The example uses factory Key A (FF FF FF FF FF FF); it cannot read block 4 if this card uses another sector 1 key. Keep the card still, or try a fresh test tag. Other tag families need their own memory commands.

R5.commandsIntro: Run the named script from Code. For R7 and R8, type the commands at the MicroPython REPL after the script starts. The grey label shows where each action happens.
R5.title: Write & verify
R5.heading: Write a test data location
R5.goal: Read existing data, explicitly arm a write to a disposable tag, then verify the new bytes.
R5.goalLine: Verify a write to Classic block 4 or Type 2 page 8.
goalCheck: The first run prints old bytes and changes nothing.

0.title: How write and readback work
body: R5 first reads the chosen user-data location. With ARM_WRITE = False it stops there; no write command is sent. Classic block 4 needs sector 1 authentication before either reading or writing.

After you explicitly set ARM_WRITE = True, the script writes 16 bytes to Classic block 4 or 4 bytes to Type 2 page 8. It reads the same location again and prints verified: True only when the bytes match.

0.does: Reads the original data and leaves the tag unchanged.
0.see: The old bytes and Read-only pass complete appear.

1.does: Writes the example bytes to the disposable tag and reads them back for comparison.
1.see: After: shows the new bytes and verified: True.

steps: Unplug USB. Set PN532 V3 switch 1 ON and switch 2 OFF. Wire the four I²C pins as in R1. Open Code, install pn532.py once, and connect the MicroPython REPL.
Reinstall the updated pn532.py on the board. Use a disposable tag you own. Run rfid_r5_pn532.py with ARM_WRITE = False and record old data.
Set ARM_WRITE = True, rerun with the same tag and check readback.
R5.note: This overwrites Classic block 4 (16 bytes) or Type 2 page 8 (4 bytes). It never writes manufacturer or lock data or Classic sector trailers. For PN532 status 0x14, enter a known sector 1 key in CLASSIC_KEY; no bytes are changed when authentication fails. Reset ARM_WRITE to False afterward.

R6.commandsIntro: Run the named script from Code. For R7 and R8, type the commands at the MicroPython REPL after the script starts. The grey label shows where each action happens.
R6.title: Field edge
R6.heading: Measure the PN532 field edge
R6.goal: Measure detection rate and read time at four card positions.
R6.goalLine: Record hits out of ten at four measured positions.
goalCheck: The script prints four hit counts and average scan times.
Moving beyond range lowers the hit count.

0.title: How the field test works
body: At each of four positions the script runs ten card-detection attempts. It counts successful reads and measures the time spent scanning, then prints hits out of ten and the average scan time.

Keep the same tag and orientation while changing only its position. The PN532 result does not include signal strength, so the hit count is the practical indication of the field edge in this experiment.

0.does: Measures ten scans at each of four card positions.
0.see: Four lines report hits/10 and average milliseconds per scan.

steps: Unplug USB. Set PN532 V3 switch 1 ON and switch 2 OFF. Wire the four I²C pins as in R1. Open Code, install pn532.py once, and connect the MicroPython REPL.
Run rfid_r6_pn532.py with one tag.
At each prompt hold it still: flat, 1 cm, 2 cm and near the edge. Record hits/10.
R6.note: The passive target response has no RSSI. Hits per ten scans is the observable metric; distance depends on tag and orientation.

R7.commandsIntro: Run the named script from Code. For R7 and R8, type the commands at the MicroPython REPL after the script starts. The grey label shows where each action happens.
R7.title: Card manager
R7.heading: Manage a simulated door locally
R7.goal: Store a UID allowlist on the C5, enroll cards, block one and print access decisions in the console.
R7.goalLine: See GRANTED for an enrolled card, then DENIED after blocking it.
goalCheck: check changes from GRANTED to DENIED after block UID.

0.title: How the simulated door decides
body: The PN532 reads a card UID; the C5 looks it up in rfid_r7_cards.json. Enrolling adds a name and an allowed state, while blocking changes that saved state.
The check command prints GRANTED only for an enrolled, unblocked UID. The decision stays in the REPL; this exercise does not control a physical lock. The JSON file preserves the list after a restart.

0.does: Reads the tapped UID and saves it with the name Ada in the local allowlist.
0.see: Enrolled appears with the UID and name.

1.does: Looks up the tapped UID and its blocked state.

2.does: Marks that saved UID as blocked in the local file.
2.see: The REPL prints block and the UID.

3.does: Checks the same card against the updated allowlist.

steps: Unplug USB. Set PN532 V3 switch 1 ON and switch 2 OFF. Wire the four I²C pins as in R1. Open Code, install pn532.py once, and connect the MicroPython REPL.
Run rfid_r7_pn532.py. Type enroll Ada and tap a card.
Type check and tap it again. Copy its UID from list, run block UID, and check again.
Rerun the script to confirm the list survives.
R7.note: This is a classroom simulation and does not actuate a lock. The list is in rfid_r7_cards.json. A UID can be copied, so this is unsuitable for real access control. The older Arduino door-app uses a different protocol.

R8.commandsIntro: Run the named script from Code. For R7 and R8, type the commands at the MicroPython REPL after the script starts. The grey label shows where each action happens.
R8.title: Card friends
R8.heading: Give each card a persistent friend
R8.goal: Map UIDs to eight characters in the C5 filesystem. Two taps print a joint scene cue.
R8.goalLine: Assign two cards different friends and make a TOGETHER line.
goalCheck: A second card prints TOGETHER with both names.

0.title: How card friends are remembered
body: The PN532 reads a UID and the C5 associates it with one of eight character names in rfid_r8_friends.json. The character is stored on the board, so the tag itself is never written.

Each tap prints a FRIEND line. The script also remembers the previous UID; when you tap a different card next, it prints a TOGETHER line with both characters. Reloading the script reads the saved assignments.

0.does: Assigns the fox character to the tapped UID and saves the mapping.
0.see: A FRIEND line contains that UID and fox.

1.does: Assigns robot to another UID and remembers the previous card.
1.see: The next FRIEND line is followed by TOGETHER,fox,robot.

2.does: Reads the saved UID-to-character assignments from the board.
2.see: Both cards and their character names appear after a restart.

steps: Unplug USB. Set PN532 V3 switch 1 ON and switch 2 OFF. Wire the four I²C pins as in R1. Open Code, install pn532.py once, and connect the MicroPython REPL.
Run rfid_r8_pn532.py. Type give fox and tap card 1; type give robot and tap card 2.
Type tap for each in turn. Check FRIEND and TOGETHER, then rerun and inspect list.
R8.note: The character lives in rfid_r8_friends.json on the board, not in tag memory. This MicroPython script prints scene cues; the older Arduino friends-app uses a different firmware protocol.
